title: Bernie Sanders Wants to Ban Superintelligence. What It Means for Microsoft and Amazon
excerpt: Senator Bernie Sanders and Representative Greg Casar announced forthcoming legislation on September 3 that would permanently ban artificial superintelligence...
content_html:
Senator Bernie Sanders and Representative Greg Casar announced forthcoming legislation on September 3 that would permanently ban artificial superintelligence and temporarily pause advanced AI development until a federal regulator sets safety rules. The proposal would also direct the United States to pursue international agreements and establish penalties for violations. Microsoft Corporation (NASDAQ:MSFT) and Amazon.com, Inc. (NASDAQ:AMZN) are central because they finance frontier models, sell cloud compute, and build their own AI products.

Microsoft's bull case is enterprise distribution. Azure, Copilot, and its model partnerships can turn large infrastructure investments into recurring software and cloud revenue. A safety regulator could even favor a scaled vendor with compliance staff, identity controls, and established government relationships. The bear case is that a broad definition of advanced AI could delay model releases, strand capacity, or raise compliance costs before legislators agree on measurable thresholds.

Northfoto / Shutterstock.com

Insider Monkey counted 273 hedge funds holding Microsoft Corporation (NASDAQ:MSFT) at June 30, down from 282 at March 31. Peter Rathjens, Bruce Clarke, and John Campbell's Arrowstreet Capital disclosed 27,659,541 shares after increasing its position by 14%. The quarter-end filing predates the bill announcement.

Amazon's exposure runs through AWS, Bedrock, custom Trainium chips, and its $18 billion minority investment in Anthropic. Its bull case is model choice and infrastructure efficiency: customers can use several providers while AWS earns from compute. Its bear case is the roughly $220 billion of 2026 capital spending that management expects to monetize over years.A regulatory pause could lengthen that payback or push workloads overseas.

Three hundred sixty-nine hedge funds held Amazon.com, Inc. (NASDAQ:AMZN) in Q2, up from 353 in Q1. Arrowstreet reported 40,346,851 shares, 24% more than in the prior quarter.

Microsoft's August 14 short-interest settlement showed 68,544,953 shares sold short, equal to 0.92% of float, with 2.05 days to cover. The low reading suggests little structural short positioning before the proposal. The bill text had not been released when the sponsors announced it, and its support is uncertain, so investors should not treat a ban as enacted policy. The immediate effect is a larger policy discount on frontier spending. The durable tests are statutory definitions, regulator authority, international coordination, and whether compliance slows smaller rivals more than the cloud incumbents. A regulator could also force clearer capability testing and incident reporting, raising fixed costs but improving customer trust. The risk becomes financially material only when rules change deployment schedules, utilization, or product eligibility. That distinction should anchor near-term valuation debates.
